lesson.title: Vulnerability Meets Trigger: The Diathesis-Stress Model
lesson.summary: The diathesis-stress model explains the onset of many psychological disorders as the combination of an underlying vulnerability, called a diathesis, and a triggering life stressor, where either factor alone is often not enough to produce disorder.
lesson.body:
A diathesis is a predisposition or vulnerability toward a disorder. It can be genetic, biological, such as a particular neurochemical sensitivity, or psychological, such as a temperament prone to rumination or negative emotionality. Stress, in this model, refers to a triggering event or ongoing life circumstance, a major loss, a trauma, chronic hardship, or another significant stressor of the kind covered in earlier material on stress and behavior. The model's core claim is that disorder tends to emerge specifically at the intersection of the two, not from either one by itself.

A simple example illustrates the logic. Imagine two people who each experience the same painful loss. One person has a family history suggesting a genetic vulnerability toward depression, combined with a temperament that tends toward rumination. The other person does not carry that same vulnerability. The diathesis-stress model predicts the first person faces meaningfully higher risk of developing depression following that loss, not because the stressor alone caused it, since most people who experience loss do not develop a diagnosable disorder, and not because the vulnerability alone caused it, since many people carrying that same vulnerability never develop the disorder absent a significant trigger, but because of how the two factors combined in that particular case.

This is best understood as a specific, mechanism-level version of biopsychosocial thinking. The diathesis side usually blends biological and psychological factors, of the kind explored in earlier material on heredity and behavior, including evidence from family and twin studies on how vulnerabilities can run in families. The stress side usually arrives through the social or environmental route. So the diathesis-stress model is essentially one concrete account of how biopsychosocial threads causally interact to produce disorder onset in a particular person at a particular time, rather than merely co-occurring.

An important nuance worth holding onto: this model helps explain why disorder is not simply caused by a stressful event, since most people who go through hardship do not develop a disorder, and also not simply caused by genes or vulnerability alone, since many vulnerable people never develop a disorder either. The framework is widely used across a range of conditions, including mood disorders, anxiety disorders, and schizophrenia, though the specific vulnerabilities and stressors involved differ by disorder and remain active areas of ongoing research.
